maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1965-66 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1966 was presented by Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1965-66 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should make a short statement. There is no need for detailed comment concerning these main estimates because they are identical with those which I tabled in this House during the previous session of Parliament. Because they were distributed to all members of Parliament at that time, I have not arranged for another general distribution now.
On that occasion, which was March 22, I made a short statement which can be found on pages 12,607 and 12,608 of Hansard for the second session of this Parliament. Tables related to the estimates were included in Hansard on pages 12,609, 12,610 and 12,611. Opposition spokesmen made their usual statements at that time also.
During the previous session Parliament provided interim supply for April and May by the enactment of Appropriation Act No. 1, 1965, based on estimates identical to those which I have tabled today. These estimates will provide the basis for further votes of supply during this session to provide for 1965-66 requirements.
I should draw the attention of the House to a discrepancy on page 5 of these estimates. The total amount shown in the summary for "Loans, Investments and Advances" should read $201,994,800, as printed on page 524, rather than $202,144,800 as shown in the summary. The correct figure which appears on page 524 will be the one considered by the Committee of Supply.
["Mr. Speaker, I shall be very happy to pass along these words of congratulation and thanks, and may I express my hope that conditions will rapidly improve in the hon. Member's constituency."]

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That the message of His Excellency, together with the estimates presented this day, be referred to the Committee of Supply.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this proposed legislation envisages a situation whereby Senators will hold their places in the Senate until the age of 75 years is attained, rather than for life as at present. It is proposed that this situation be brought about by the following method: First, that any person summoned to the Senate after the coming into force of this legislation would be subject to compulsory retirement at the age of 75 years. Senators who are now holding their places in the Senate would not be interfered with. However, they would be given the option of retiring with an adequate retiring allowance, if they so wished, on attaining the age of 75 years, or if by reason of health they were unable to carry on.
In other words there are three distinct parts to the legislation. The first part would deal with the amendment of section 29 of the British North America Act to provide for the retirement at age 75 of persons summoned to the Senate in the future. Part two will consist of a series of amendments extending the provisions of the present Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, which now is applicable only to members of the House of Commons, to those members of the Senate who are summoned to the Senate in the future. These persons will be subject to the same retiring allowance legislation as are members of the House of Commons at the present time.
The third part of the proposals envisaged in the legislation is a series of provisions which will apply to Senators already holding their places in the Senate or who are appointed to the Senate before the coming into force of the proposed legislation. These latter provisions will make it possible for Senators who attain the age of 75 years or who have become permanently disabled to resign their places in the Senate and be granted an annuity eaual to two thirds of their indemnity. Provision would also be made for an annuity to be granted to the widow of a Senator who during his lifetime had been granted an an-
DEBATES	409
Retirement Age for Senators nuity under the Bill. This would make it possible for such a Senator to resign his place in the Senate with the assurance that if he died, his widow would be provided for. Thus in effect the legislation would provide that future Senators would contribute to a pension scheme in the same manner as members of the House of Commons, and that persons now in the Senate would have an option of retiring with non-contributory annuities similar to those provided for judges.
Now, Mr. Chairman, having outlined the purpose of the legislation and the method being sought to be used, I do not think there is much I can usefully add at this resolution stage. If there are any questions, I will be glad to try to answer them, but I think the three general points are fairly clear, simple and direct, and that the more detailed provisions can be better examined when we see the legislation after the Bill itself is put before the house.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF RETIREMENT AGE FOR SENATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say at once of this resolution that one might almost term it a fiddling with Senate reform. Indeed, it is simply a generality, that those appointed to the Senate hereafter shall retire at the age of 75, but that no action will be taken among the Senators today occupying that high and august position.
I recall immediately that when we were in office we decided that there should be an age limit of 75, effective for new appointments and for incumbents. It is of interest to recall that on April 9, 1962 I, as the then Prime Minister, moved for leave to introduce a Bill to amend the British North America Act in respect of the Senate. I stated, as reported at page 2607 of Hansard for that date:
The amendment which will be brought before the House will be restricted to retirement at the age of 75 years of all members in the other place, as well as those who may thereafter be appointed. Provision will be made for a retirement pension for all who are now in the Senate. A resolution to that effect will be placed on the order paper today. I think I should also make it clear now that in the event that this amendment is passed, no appointment of successors to vacancies resulting from the compulsory retirement of Senators under this legislation will be made until after the next general election.
That was the purport and summary of the measures we had in mind. We made it very clear that there would be no appointments made of successors to those who would be automatically retired until after the next election.
First reading of the bill was opposed by the hon. Member for Kootenay West, and the
410	COMMONS

The Bill, first reading of which was agreed to, stated simply as follows:
Section 29 of the British North America Act, 1867 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"A Senator shall, subject to this Act, hold his place in the Senate until he attains the age of seventy-five years or until the coming into force of this section if at that time he has already attained that age."
The the Bill was described. At the same time, Mr. Chairman, there was a bill to provide for the payment of annuities to persons who had served as members of the Senate, immediately after each and every Senator to which the act applied ceased to hold office.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Now, Sir, the legislation that is envisaged by the resolution is simply a milk and water substitute for the promises that have been made for so many years. One has only to look back a matter of 46 years ago when Senate reform was promised during the 1919 convention of the Liberal Party. I recall very well the election of 1925 when the then Prime Minister, Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, stated that reform of the Senate was a first and a foremost course of action needed to assure democracy in this country. He said the same thing in 1926. I recall so well the promises of that day. He said he was going to substitute live Grits for dead Tories in the Senate. Some of those appointed were only half qualified on the basis of Mr. King's description.
Again in 1935 he was going to reform the Senate. You will recall that he stated that each and every Senator appointed would sign a declaration to the effect that he would voluntarily remove himself at any time that the Prime Minister decided. We do not know how many actually entered into that form of undertaking. On several occasions we endeavoured to secure copies of these resignations in anticipation but nobody was ever able to see them. We tried in 1944, as I recall, and again without success.
What of this measure now before us? Sir, this is simply a watered down type of reform.
It is interesting to read about the Senate.
It was to provide a sober, second thought. On many occasions throughout the years it has justified its existence. It has stood against an all-powerful House of Commons when

Then he goes on to deal with the real question. I am citing Mr. Hutchison's view to the Prime Minister because Mr. Hutchison has become a monitor to the Government. He went on to say:

I am not going into the list of appointments that have been made unless, of course, I am provoked into doing so, but certainly in the appointments that have been made by the present Government there is no indication that the admonitions and advice given by that extracurricular adviser have been carried out. The canniest politicians try to protect their rear by making their actions conform as closely as possible to their past pronouncements.

I think there would be no particular objection taken by Canadians as a whole if two or three outstanding appointments were made from that body. I would suggest a measure of reform that could be made would be the designating, to a

No, Mr. Chairman, I would not and I made that clear earlier. It would be quite impossible to designate the Senate as a place in which money bills could be introduced. If we were to follow that course we would deprive the House of Commons of its inherent and exclusive right to control money matters. Many other types of legislation could be introduced there and the fullest examination could take place. I, of course, make it very clear, and I am sure the Prime Minister agrees, that there would be no justification whatever for the introduction in that Chamber of measures in the nature of money Bills.
So far as what is introduced here is concerned, I do not think it is of great importance. It is a step, a faltering step. Those who are going to be appointed hereafter will automatically retire at 75. Those who are over 75 can stay if they choose. It is interesting that an appointment to that body seems to be a tremendous encouragement to longevity. Few, if any, of the Senators who are over 75 will retire. Why should they, when they are going to get the indemnity that today is available? Why was it that action was not taken to make effective the retirement at 75? Well, I can only conclude there was a fear on the part of the Government that such a measure might receive opposition in the other place. This is scarcely a sound qualification for the determination of Government policy.
This is simply legislation that makes a step forward, but it is innocuous in so far as being effective today is concerned. However, half a loaf is better than none. What is before the House is merely a shadow of what was contemplated 46 years ago at the Liberal convention. However, 46 years is not a long time to wait for the implementation of Liberal policy.

speechtext:
At any rate, apart from any difference in the effective retirement date, that is the only reform either of them proposed, namely that some Senators retire at age 75. The Leader of the Opposition suggests that half a loaf is better than no bread at all. I am not so sure that this measure is to be regarded in that light. It strikes me that it is the kind of measure that might fool the Canadian people into thinking that something had been done to reform the Senate, and therefore it would be another 46 years before something might be done again.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, if we are going to consider the Senate at all, we ought to come up to date; we ought to recognize that we are in the 1960's. We ought to ask ourselves whether there is any place in our parliamentary institution for a group of people who are not responsible to the electors of this country. I can understand the thinking of the Fathers of Confederation 100 years ago. In that day they believed in democracy, but not completely. There was a lingering notion that in addition to those who are elected by the people there should be some elder statesmen, like the Members of the House of Lords of the United Kingdom, who would have the final say, a veto, a chance to check on the work of the elected Members. But, Mr. Chairman, we have moved a bit in the last 100 years. We no longer think that the elected people have to be vetoed, or checked, or supervised by people who are not elected. In our view the House of Commons, consisting of Members elected by the people of Canada, should be the final court so far as the making of laws is concerned.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I am putting this forward in a very low key. I do not need to shout our position from the housetops because it has been well known

throughout the years of the C.C.F. and since the founding of the New Democratic Party, namely, that we believe the Senate ought to be abolished. We think that any measure of reform, particularly so ineffective a measure as this, is hardly worth the time it takes us to deal with it.
I know the arguments in favour of having the Senate. With 23 other Members of the House of Commons I had the experience during the Christmas recess of sitting on a joint committee which had 12 members from the other place, and I know their contributions to the work of that committee were very useful. I also know that from time to time the Senate sets up interesting and useful committees. They had one on employment a while ago, one on the use of land, and one on aging. These are all good committees and their Honours do interesting and useful work. But this is the kind of work to be done by people appointed for that purpose, and ought not to be done by people who enjoy the same status that the elected representatives do, but with the additional right to veto legislation passed by the people's elected representatives.
Perhaps because in the United Kingdom the House of Lords cannot finally veto legislation, but can only delay its passage, or perhaps from the fact that in the United States the veto of the President can be overridden by a two thirds vote of the two houses of Congress, -whatever the origin-there is a notion held generally in Canada that the Senate can only go so far, that it can only turn down legislation once, twice or three times, or something like that.
However, the constitutional position is that the Senate could block a measure passed by the House, year after year, to the end of time. I know this has never happened. I know that the number of times the Senate has vetoed something passed in the House of Commons has been very limited. The outstanding example is the first old age pensions Act back in 1926, and two or three matters in the years from 1957 to 1963. I know the Senate does not do this very often, but it has, as a constitutional entitlement, the right to say no to what the people's elected representatives have decided. In terms of political theory, in terms of democratic practice, I think this is wrong, and that we should be taking a serious look at the position of a non-elected body in our parliamentary institution.
Another point sometimes made is that the Senators are there to protect minority rights, and in particular to protect provincial rights.
April 26, 1965

I suggest however that that is no more their function than it is the function of the House of Commons and also that of the courts. 1 further suggest that we have had the Senate for 98 years, that our Federal-Provincial situation is not all that it might be, and that having the Senate has not taken care of that problem.
It seems to me that all the various arguments for the retention of a second House, particularly a non-elected one, fall to the ground, and that what the House of Commons, should have placed before it on this occasion is not some measure of ineffective reform but rather a measure for the abolition of the Senate.
Hon. Members are aware I have such a bill on the Order Paper as a private Members' public bill, but it does not have quite the same chance of being reached, let alone the chance of being voted on, as a Government measure has.
As I have said, these arguments have been stated time and time again. They are frequently the subject of debate in high schools and universities. The subject has frequently come up here, and before we proceed with a measure of this kind I submit this is the kind of consideration we ought to be giving the subject.
I see, Mr. Chairman, that you are fidgeting a bit. Maybe it is just in my mind, but I wonder if perhaps you were thinking I was getting away from the subject of the resolution by talking about the abolition of the Senate, when all we have before us is a limited measure of Senate reform. But I want to make it clear that I do not agree with the position of the Leader of the Opposition, namely that by reforming the Senate we should be giving it more responsibility, more voice and more legislation. Members of the other place, fine ladies and gentlemen that they are, are not elected by the people of Canada and I do not think they should have the role in our parliamentary institution that is accorded them by our constitution-and I believe that is the change we ought to be making, namely the abolition of the Senate itself.
I should now like to say a word or two about the specific terms of the resolution, and particularly about the outline of those terms as given to us by the President of the Privy Council. I not that the Bill is to have three main parts and that the first part is to carry out the main proposal, to provide for an amendment to the British North America Act whereby all persons appointed to the
Retirement Age for Senators Senate after the passage of this legislation shall be compulsorily retired at age 75. As I have already said, that is an ineffective piece of legislation that does not really amount to anything, in the face of what ought to be done.
The second part of the proposed Bill is to make provision for those who, having been appointed after the coming into effect of this legislation will be compelled to retire at 75, to give them the rights and privileges that Members of the House of Commons enjoy under the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act. I suppose if Members are going to be summoned to the Senate for a limited period of time, and if we are in an age when we feel that all classes of employment should have certain pension rights, then Members of the Senate appointed under these conditions should also have pension rights. But I want to object-and I ask the Prime Minister to listen to me on this-I want to object most strongly to what has been indicated as part III of the bill.
If I heard the President of the Privy Council correctly he said that provision would be made for those who are now in the Senate, and those who are appointed between now and the time the Bill becomes law, on reaching 75 to retire voluntarily on a pension that I understand will be non-contributory, a free pension equal to two-thirds of their present indemnity. The present indemnity of a Senator is $12,000 a year. Two thirds of that is $8,000 a year. We are therefore saying to any Senator who is now for example 50 years of age that for the next 25 years he gets an indemnity of $12,000, plus his $3,000 expense allowance; and then, at age 75, without having contributed one nickel to a pension fund he can retire, if he wishes to do so, on an $8,000 pension, plus provision for a widow's pension if he should die after he goes on that pension. Let me divorce all of this, however, from what I am saying about the Senate as an institution. I think it should go. Apparently I cannot carry that idea today, so I have to deal with the situation as it is. I feel that in present situation, when we in this house have a pension plan to which we contribute, when we have just set up a Canada Pension Plan on a contributory basis and when it is accepted by most people that pensions are theirs as a right, because they have earned them by working for them and paying for them, to pick out this particular group of men and women and say "You do not have to pay one cent for this; if you do us the favour of

Even though I have said many critical things about the Senate as an institution, I know a good many of them over there; there are many decent, upright and honourable people in the other place and I think most of them would agree in principle that they should pay for their pensions, just as we have to pay for ours. If they do not agree with this proposition I suggest they should not be given this pension as a bribe.
Speaking of the general situation there is, of course, provision for widows' pensions. This is a matter which, I know, concerns some of the Senators. When a Senator dies there is nothing for his widow. But if the pension, even if it had to be paid for, included a widow's pension, Senators might take a different view toward it than is now the case. When I looked at the resolution I wondered whether it was in effect an attempt to bribe Senators to vote in favour of the measure, but even I was not suspicious enough to think that this was the case. However, the question asked by the President of the Privy Council makes it clear that this is a bribe as the Government sees it. The Government wants to get this measure through. It wants some of the Senators to retire at the age of 75 and it has decided that the only way to accomplish this is to offer them a free pension of $8,000 at age 75. In a day when we have not yet got the old age security pension up to $100 a month or $1,200 a year; in a day when we have not found it possible to increase the pensions of retired civil servants or retired employees of the Canadian National Railways; in a day when, despite various improvements, we are still struggling with the problem of providing adequate pensions for our people, I do not think this Parliament should approve offering to those who have enjoyed indemnities for a lengthy period of time the kind of annuity which is now suggested. I do not think this phase of the legislation should receive the support of the House
April 26. 1965

and I hope that before the Bill is brought down the Government will take a further look at this aspect of it.
We think this is a case of fiddling with Senate reform in an ineffective way. What should be done is to provide for its abolition so that our Parliament can be a truly democratic institution composed only of men and women elected by the citizens of Canada.

I must say I am very disappointed by the resolution before us. I fail to understand why the Government should have taken such a "milquetoast" approach to this question. This is nothing but a minute and timid attempt to initiate a measure of Senate reform. Possibly the Government did not wish to come forward with proposals for a major overhaul; but why did it not bring forward at least one or two firm proposals indicative of a desire to correct some of the faults and shortcomings of the institution which we refer to as the other place? I urge the Government to amend its intentions, at least as they concern this phase of the resolution respecting the retirement of future Senators at the age of 75.
I have many good friends in the Senate and I highly respect many of the men and women who compose that body. I believe they have a worth-while contribution to make. From my conversations with them I would say that most of them have no objection to constructive proposals. They realize that the institution is antiquated. I cannot understand what pressures on the Government would result in the bringing forward of a bill which has so little backbone. If the establishment of a retirement age is a legitimate part of Senate reform, why not make it effective now? In recognition of the fact that no provision has been made for Senators who retire, it would be logical to make some provision. I do not go along with the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre when he says they have not made any contribution-they have not had a chance to contribute. His suggestion may be something for the future. But even if they were retired at $8,000 a year now, that would save the Government of Canada $7,000 a year per Senator.

We are talking now about setting the retirement at age 75. I really do hope that the Government are not going to bring in a Bill that is as insipid as this resolu-
415
Retirement Age for Senators tion indicates it is going to be. I do not think this is the time for entering into any lengthy debate on Senatorial reform, although I find it very amusing to listen to the Leader of the Official Opposition as he talks about what he had once planned to do. Certainly if he had wanted to bring in Senatorial reform long ago, he would have done it while he was in office. I do not think there has been any Prime Minister of Canada who has made such political use out of the Senate as did the former Prime Minister, now the Leader of the Official Opposition. I do not think there is much argument as far as concerns what should have been done in the past, but we must have our eyes to the future.
I for one certainly am not in favour of the abolition of the Senate. I think the Senate has a very important role to play, and I think we must be very cautious in taking an irrevocable stand on saying that even an appointed Senate does not have a responsible role. There are some advantages in an appointed Senate that an elected Senate cannot have. But on the other hand, to suggest that the Senate in its present state of affairs is anything but an antiquated piece of machinery that no longer fills a very useful role, or that it should be perpetuated even until future Senators reach 75 years of age is not, I think, putting on coloured glasses; it is just putting on glasses that cannot be seen through at all-because certainly there are some changes that should be brought into the Senatorial picture.
I think that one of the tragedies and certainly one of the weaknesses of the present Senate is that it does not properly represent political opinion, thinking and action in the various Provinces. Certainly it has not brought into the Senate the best qualified individuals in Canada who might have been, if the Senate had operated on any other basis than being a political arm of the particular party which was responsible for government. I would have hoped that at this stage the Government would have taken some step which would have made Provincial representation in the Senate possible. It is the prerogative of the Federal Government to appoint Senators; but what a tremendous opportunity there would have been toward establishing a greater sense of political unity if the Government were to have set up a Senatorial Commission, perhaps of three people, one representing the Government, one from the Senate itself and one appointed by the Government of the Province which was concerned in any specific Senatorial appointment
April 26, 1965

Retirement Age for Senators How much stronger and how much more representative of Canadian thinking and public opinion the Senate would have been if there had been representation of Provincial Governments in the Senate.
I think another point that really is basic, and does not get into many of the more detailed problems that a complete Senatorial overhaul would require is action which would have eliminated the conflict of interest which now besets many of our Senators as they serve in the Senate. Why should they not be subject to the same restrictions, so far as a dual interest or a conflict of interest is concerned, as we are in this House? There was no better example of this than the recent Senatorial Committee on Banking which dealt with three different bills that would have set up or given authority to the establishment of three new banks in Canada. It so happened that the majority, if not all, of the members of that Senatorial Banking Committee were themselves members of the boards of directors of other banks already in existence. It seems to me that included in this legislation could very well have been the requirement that Senators have the same restrictions placed upon them which was intended to eliminate conflict of interest in so far as their public responsibilities are concerned.
I think that likewise if the Government had been concerned about the welfare of the Senators who hold appointments at the present time they might have set up some machinery by which a pension could have been provided for those who retire before they reach 75 years of age. In other words, there is nothing wrong at all with a contributory pension scheme for those who might be appointed under any new system of appointment.
I think another point that would have been very important here would have been to bring some attendance requirement into the Senate. All that is necessary now is that a Senator appear once in any session. Why should not Senators be required to fill a minimum requirement as far as attendance and participation are concerned, as we do in this House? These are small things, Mr. Chairman, that would not have required amendments to the British North America Act, which would have been a positive step toward an over-all Senatorial reform pattern *and which could have been included in this legislation. I believe such action would have indicated to the Canadian people that the Government really was sincere in its inten-
IMr. Thompson.]
tion of bringing in Senatorial reforms. As it is now, this insipid suggestion that is supposed to give benefit a little later on really has not any worth whatsoever to it. It is a sham or a cover-over in order to make the people of Canada think there has been some step taken toward reforming the Senate.
I am concerned, as one who believes that the Senate has a place, that the whole purpose and usefulness of the Senate in the eyes of public opinion has been weakened, and if continued in this way it might well lead us to a point where public opinion will demand the abolition of the Senate. I think this certainly would not be in the best interests of the country. I would like to see Senate appointments set up through a Senatorial Commission, not only so this Commission could consider the recommendations of the Provinces but also that Senators appointed would represent the Provinces as well as the Federal Government, and also making possible non-partisan political appointments. Men and women selected because of their own service to Canada and their own abilities on the Canadian scene in the non-political fields would make the Senate of much more worth. I am thinking of men in education, men in business, retired civil servants-yes, even retired military personnel-and men in the arts. All these people, if they had an opportunity to come into the Senate free of any partisan political influence, would make the Senate certainly a much more effective, much more efficient and much more useful institution.

Mr. Chairman, this resolution is some sort of a draft for the bill which will be introduced here eventually.
I thought it would contain other provisions than the one setting the retirement age of senators at 75, giving present incumbents the choice of retaining their seat even if they are past the age of retirement or to retire with full benefits as far as pension and other benefits are concerned if they have reached the age of 75.
How many senators are 75 or more at present? I should like to have a reply from the President of the Privy Council on that point.
On the other hand, I would suggest that if the bill to be introduced provides for retirement of senators at the age of 75, that provision apply to everyone whether one wants to retire or not. I even find that 75 is a rather advanced age; it should be 70. But there are many, or at least I believe there are some, who are beyond that age limit who have perhaps been improvident-although many there are very well off-and who took the employment in the belief that it was theirs for life, and that therefore they did not have to make other financial provision for a different type of livelihood when they had finished with it, who could not now support themselves, their wives or their families in anywhere near the manner to which they have grown accustomed. In fact there may be some who would find it extremely difficult to support their families in any fitting manner whatsoever. I think, then, to suggest, when it is said that we must do something for these

people, that we are being unkind to call it a bribe, is perhaps not facing the realities of the situation. However, I am a little suspicious that this is a very small minority of those who would be affected.
From my personal knowledge of the Senate-and I am afraid I have not had the opportunity or the pleasure of getting to know as many as I would like, and of those I do know, there are some whose financial affairs I do not know very well-but from what I have gathered from meeting Senators and from talks with my colleagues, a great many Members of the Senate are not at all in need of financial assistance. That is an argument, of course, against the necessity for offering them a bribe. If a man is not in need of financial assistance, then a pension would hardly seem to be an effective bribe to offer him. It is only the person who needs a pension that would need, perhaps not a bribe to make up his mind, but a way in which it becomes economically possible for him to follow the expressed wish of Parliament. I think that is a very important distinction. I like to liken it to the difference between convicting the man who is innocent and letting guilty people go free.
It is a most important maxim of our law, in the conduct of our criminal courts, that it is better that ten guilty persons should go free than one innocent person should be punished. I think, in fairness to the President of the Privy Council, before we use the word "bribe" we should perhaps use this type of reasoning; that even if there were only one or two Senators whose retirement might be in the best interests of the country, because they are over age-and I suggest that those who are over age and should retire are perhaps not aware that it is they themselves who are the weak ones in the House- it makes it only just, and not terrible, that we should make it financially possible for them to retire; because when they took on the job it was a contract between them and the Government of a job for life. I do not suppose in the years to come that there will be anything that this Party sitting on the other side, this great Canadian Party which has given such leadership to this country for so many years, will be so ashamed of as this proposal. I do not know for how many years-one would have to search the records-they have talked of Senate reform. Their great leaders, like Mr. Mackenzie King, could talk out of both sides of their mouths so ably that you could quote them on any subject; but they have told us what they would do and how they would do it. And what do we have here, Mr. Chairman? A proposal to bring in a bill which from now on means, after the bill is passed, that Senators will have to retire at age 75. But those great people now in the Senate can stay on or retire on an annuity of $8,000 a year.
I do not suppose in the history of Canada that there has been a worse group of Senators appointed to the upper chamber than those appointed by this Government in the short period of time it has been in office.

I am surprised by this, because there are some people in Canada who are Liberal Party supporters who do have ability. One has only to look at the universities of Canada to find a professor of history, or a professor of economics, or a doctor who is a Liberal. One would think, after all the fine speeches which have been made on the other side of
Retirement Age for Senators the House, that some of these good people could have been appointed to the Senate since this Government took office so that they could have raised the standard of ability and quality in the other House.
I am not going to go into details today, but before this legislation passes we are going to put on the record the kind of people who have been appointed. One of the new Members is a very young man-I will not mention his name-who is still in his early forties. What is his great distinction, and the quality for which he has been appointed to the Senate-to a post where, as there seems to be something about the Senate which is conducive to old age, being in his early forties he can sit for another 40 years? What is his great quality or ability, this great service he can render to the Canadian people? He was the fund raiser in charge of the pork barrel of the Liberal Party in Ontario, which really makes him a good person to put in the Senate of Canada. That it the kind of person who has been appointed, Mr. Chairman.
What we have to realize with our present set-up, which will be such as long as this country is unfortunate enough to have the party opposite in power, is that we have a Senate, a second chamber, which has the kind of power which no other second chamber, to my knowledge, has in any other parliamentary system in the world. After all, in Great Britain, about whose customs and history we are so proud and which we emulate so often, in words if not in spirit, it is now almost 100 years, certainly more than 50, since the power of the House of Lords was clipped. The power of the House of Lords is very limited. I am speaking from memory, and I will go into this in detail at the appropriate time, but in the passage of legislation the matter becomes law on the second presentation to the House of Lords, whether that chamber agrees with it or not. But in Canada the Senate has practically as much power as the House of Commons.
These Senators are people who are appointed for life, many of them with very little qualifications. They have the right, the opportunity and the ability to stop cold legislation which the elected House of Commons may want to pass. Let this Government have the courage-which it has not-to propose a real medicare plan and you will see pressure brought upon the Senate from insurance companies and medical associations to cut the guts out of such a plan. And what will this

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Government do it it ever has the courage to bring that kind of legislation before the Senate? Nothing.
I would have thought that before this Government brought in this proposal it could have learned something from the Province of Quebec. There they have a second chamber, an appointed chamber. The government of Quebec wants to establish the principle-a very sound principle which I wish the Prime Minister would think about some time-that the second chamber should not have the power which the elected chamber has. Because the Executive Council of the Province of Quebec has refused to pass certain legislation, the Government of Quebec is going to the Queen with a proposal that the Queen enact legislation to reduce the power of the appointed Executive Council in the Province of Quebec. Why does not the Government of Canada, this so-called great Liberal Government, propose that the power of the Senate of Canada be reduced, as it has been in every other country which has a democratic system of government? They have not done so, Mr. Chairman, because they have not got the courage. They do not mind a second chamber which has the power and authority to keep in check any proposals which in future years may come from an elected House of Commons.
I should like to say on behalf of the Members of this group that not only will we oppose this resolution but that I hope, indeed I expect, that we will fight the Bill when it comes in, clause by clause. Because I think it is a farce, a disgrace and a fraud on the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means.
He said: Mr. Speaker: It gives me a great deal of satisfaction to be able to report to the House, and to the country, on the state of our economy and of our national finances. There has been a great and encouraging improvement in economic conditions, and in the state of the budget during the past two years. This robust expansion must be continued. With the budget under control, we must use our fiscal policies to achieve the nation's goals. The primary objective now is a healthy rate of sustained economic growth.

I am glad to note that all regions in Canada have shared in this expansion. The Atlantic provinces and the province of Quebec, for example, have experienced substantially increased economic activity. I believe that it is in this context of a prosperous and expanding economy, benefiting all Canadians, that we shall best succeed not only in maintaining but in strengthening the unity of our great country.

Economic Objectives
When this government first came into office we stated a number of economic objectives. Our first goal was a high level of employment for Canadians and the reduction of unemployment. The second was a high and sustainable level of economic growth. Third, we wanted a better regional balance in both employment and growth. We also wished to bring into closer balance our trade and other current international transactions. To realize these objectives, we recognized that our industry, especially our manufacturing industry, would have to become more vigorous and competitive. We expected that as unemployment was reduced and these other objectives achieved, we would also be able to move toward a balanced budget. Moreover, we sought over the long term to improve the degree of participation by Canadians in
DEBATES	427
The Budget-Mr. Gordon the ownership and direction of businesses operating within our borders and using our resources.
We may all take pride in the extent to which these goals have been achieved.
Almost half a million new jobs have been created since the spring of 1963.
Unemployment had fallen by last month to 3.9 per cent, on a seasonally adjusted basis, which is just about half the 7.7 per cent reached in the first quarter of 1961.
This improvement in employment was not confined to one or two favoured parts of Canada. During the past two years some of the most rapid increases in employment took place in those sections of the country where unemployment had been particularly high. The decline in the unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces and British Columbia was of the order of one third between the last quarter of 1962 and the last quarter of 1964; in Quebec there was a reduction of one-quarter. In Ontario and in the prairie provinces unemployment by the last quarter of 1964 was down to about 3 per cent.
We have also had a rapid increase in the Gross National Product. In the two years 1963 and 1964, the value of the nation's output increased by 6.5 per cent and 8.9 per cent, or by a total for the two-year period of about 16 per cent. Incomes have improved materially. The value of construction of all kinds increased by more than 20 per cent from 1962 to 1964, and housing starts went up from 130,000 to 166,000-that is, by more than one-quarter.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
In our dealings with other countries we have achieved a considerable improvement in our balance of trade and payments. Our deficit on current account in 1964 was less than one-third what it was at its peak in 1959.

This improvement was achieved not by restricting imports and travel by Canadians, but by a vigorous expansion of our exports. Our secondary manufacturing industry has accounted for an important part of this change.
The improvement in our international balance of payments, and indeed in our rate of economic growth in general, could not have come about if we had not been able to keep our prices and costs competitive. Canadian

Along with these improvements in the performance of the economy we have been able to bring about a dramatic improvement in the federal budget. The 1962-63 fiscal year produced a budgetary deficit of $692 million. This has been reduced to $83 million for the fiscal year just ended.
If the accounts are translated into a form more suitable for measuring their impact on the economy, that is, into terms of the national economic accounts, the change in two years is from a deficit of $399 million in 1962-63 to a surplus of $332 million in the last fiscal year-an improvement of over $700 million.
These achievements have taken place against the background of the longest period of peacetime economic expansion we have enjoyed in the present century. However, the pace of our expansion has not proceeded without faltering. There was a noticeable pause in the advance at the end of 1962.
New Policies
In no small measure the strength of the expansion, certainly since 1962, is due to the introduction of new policies. The results achieved enable us to describe them as effective policies. They include:
(a)	Strong incentives in the form of capital cost allowances to Canadian-owned manufacturing and processing companies installing new machinery and equipment.
(b)	Similar inducements, together with a three-year tax exemption, for new manufacturing and processing companies to establish in designated areas of slow growth and high unemployment.
(c)	Special arrangements to improve the efficiency of our automobile industry and to secure a fairer share of the total automotive production of North America.

Partly as a result of such policies, the Canadian economy in the past two years has expanded faster, and unemployment has been reduced further than in the United States.
It might interest hon. Members to know that in the United States last year, 1964, the total output of the economy of that country increased by 6.6 per cent. In Canada the increase was one third as much again.
In 1964 unemployment in the United States was reduced by 7 per cent. The rate of reduction in Canada was almost twice that figure.
Current Situation and Outlook
The economy is currently in a very healthy state. Unemployment is at its lowest level since 1957. Our output of goods and services is at record heights and is still rising. Prices are reasonably stable. Our international competitive position remains strong. The capacity of our industry is being used more fully. Business confidence is reflected in the highest level of capital investment we have ever had. All areas of the country, almost all types of industry and agriculture, and most groups in the community are sharing in this advance.

It is this growth in our labour force which provides the foundation for rapid economic growth in Canada. It also makes it necessary. This necessity for growth in order to put our young and rapidly growing labour force to work was the central feature of the First Annual Review of the Economic Council, published several months ago.
Economic Council Review
Honourable members will recall the main projections which the Council brought to the nation's attention: that between 1963 and 1970 Canada's labour force can be expected to grow by 2.7 per cent per year on the average; that the potential productivity of our workers- that is, output per person employed-can be expected to increase by 1.9 per cent per year; that, if the level of unemployment can be reduced to an annual national average of 3 per cent-which the Council regards as a realistic objective-and if we can catch up the lag in our productivity gains between 1957 and 1963-we can reach an average rate of growth in our production over this period of 5i per cent. The Council points out how the achievement of this rate of growth would require and make possible rapidly expanding levels of consumer expenditures, government expenditures, business investment and exports.
The realization of the true potentials of the Canadian economy is a goal which all of us can accept. The problem has been, and will always be, to develop and put into effect the kind of policies needed so that each major
The Budget-Mr. Gordon part of the economy can make its full contribution. The Council has given us helpful advice in this regard.
There are, as the Council has pointed out, some especially difficult problems before us. Canada must train and place in the right jobs an enormous number of young people if we are to achieve the potentials the Council anticipates. Industry must grow at a pace which will provide these jobs and must increase its productivity. The capital must be found which industry, and governments, will require to finance this expansion. And above all, Canadians must find, and be efficient in competing for, the domestic and foreign markets for the goods which an expanded economy will be capable of producing.
To achieve all of this will be difficult enough, but our very success in doing so will itself pose problems. A higher rate of productivity is essential to the achievement of the nations's economic potential, and its ability to compete, but it means we have to find more markets to employ our manpower. Rapidly rising production generates more employment, but it could also lead to the large deficits in international payments which the Economic Council has projected in its model. These must be avoided.
Balances of Payments
We hear a great deal these days about the balance of payments problems of our friends the British and the Americans. The British problem springs in considerable part from the strain which has been placed on their productive capacity and which their recent budget is designed to relieve. The essence of the Americans' problem is that the very large surplus they earn in trade and other current transactions is substantially less than what is needed for the large scale private investment by Americans all over the world, in addition to the requirements of defence overseas and foreign aid.
Our problem is unlike either of these. Although we still have some room in our economy for increased production without undue strain, we continue to have a deficit in our current transactions with the rest of the world. To be sure, last year we achieved a trade surplus of $700 million. But we used up this surplus and more in servicing past debts, in paying dividends to foreigners, and in making other kinds of current payments. Our current operating deficit was, I am glad to say, lower than it had been for ten years. But it is
430	COMMONS DEBATES	April 26, 1965
The Budget-Mr. Gordon
still sizeable. Furthermore, last year we exported large quantities of wheat to Russia, and we cannot count on having such large markets for our wheat on a continuing basis.
Our persistent international payments problem is apparent not only in the total size of our current account deficit, but also in its structure. Last year our current account deficit with the United States reached nearly $1.7 billion. This was largely offset by a surplus of $1.2 billion on merchandise and non-merchandise trade with the rest of the world, including the large wheat sales to communist countries. These transactions still left us with a current account deficit of $453 million which we had to finance.
In order to provide jobs to match the quite exceptional growth of our labour force we will need high levels of capital investment in the next few years, higher than the present physical capacity of the economy can be expected to meet. I do not anticipate difficulties in financing outside Canada the moderate amounts really required for this purpose, but this dependence on foreign savings should not be permitted to persist indefinitely. The world is hungry for capital for investment both in developing and in industrialized countries. The major source of capital, the United States, is having to restrict its investments abroad. We would be foolhardy if we assumed that over the long term the capital needed to cover our continuing current account deficits, whatever their size, would always be ours for the asking.
Financial Markets
The performance of our financial markets during 1964 was remarkably good. Through the first half of the year, they weathered successfully the continuing uncertainties arising out of the United States' Interest Equalization Tax. Later they adjusted readily to the disturbances arising out of the United Kingdom balance of payments problems. In spite of these difficulties the Canadian capital markets handled a greater volume of new issues than in the previous year.
The substantial improvement in the federal government's financial position enabled us to reduce our demands on the market, thereby making room for other borrowers. The improvement in the government's position also made it easier for monetary policy to continue to give support to economic expansion. Interest rates were slightly lower at the end of the year than they had been at the beginning.
The House will recall that, at the time the United States' Interest Equalization Tax and

the Canadian exemption were announced in July, 1963, the Canadian government stated its intention not to seek to increase Canadian exchange reserves through borrowing in the United States. During 1964 Canadian monetary and debt-management operations were undertaken with a view to their effect on Canadian borrowers who might seek funds in the United States, as well as with a view to domestic conditions. The interest rate differentials between Canada and the United States fell, during the course of 1964, to the lowest level for some time.
The financial disturbances at the time of the sterling crisis and the raising of the bank rate in Canada were not allowed to interfere with this development. In fact, the careful handling of that situation by the Bank of Canada considerably assisted in meeting this objective and keeping our capital market working effectively.
The past year was marked by a further evolution of the international financial machinery. Just as Canada benefited from the rapid assembly of massive financial assistance at the time of her exchange crisis in 1962, so Britain was the recipient of even more massive aid in the autumn of 1964. Canada was an active and major participant in this operation.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
International Liquidity
During the year representatives of the government took part in a series of international discussions on world liquidity. The question at issue has been whether the total of international reserves, such as our own reserves of gold and foreign exchange, when combined with official international credit arrangements such as those provided by the International Monetary Fund or by arrangements between central banks, is sufficient to support the growing level of international trade and payments both now and in the years ahead.
As Minister of Finance I attended meetings of the so-called "Group of Ten" in Paris last June and of the Board of Governors of the International Monetary Fund in Tokyo last September. The most immediate result of these discussions is that the Fund itself is to be enlarged by a 25 per cent increase in the quotas of all members, plus special additional increases for member countries such as Canada whose growth has been well above the average. I have made it quite clear that Canada would have welcomed a greater increase than this in world liquidity in order
April 26, 1965	COMMONS
to ensure expansion of world trade and payments without any drag or interruption.
Trade Policies
In the Budget Speech last year I described our preparations for the "Kennedy Round" of tariff negotiations in Geneva, and outlined the principles that would govern Canada's participation. The formal opening of the negotiations occurred last November when the offers of reductions in duties on industrial goods and materials were exchanged. Our delegation is now engaged in a detailed examination, with other delegations, of the scope for tariff reductions of mutual benefit.
The negotiations on agricultural products are only now getting under way. This means that for Canada, with its important export interests in agriculture, the Kennedy Round is not yet in full swing.
Consequently it would be premature to offer any firm or final judgment as to the probable outcome of this tariff conference. Nevertheless I believe there are real possibilities for important tariff reductions covering a broad range of our exports. We have a strong delegation in Geneva, headed by Mr. Norman Robertson, one of the most respected senior public servants of Canada. I can assure the House that our representatives will bargain vigorously and realistically to advance the interests of Canada at this conference. It is in our interests that barriers to trade throughout the world be progressively reduced.
There has been a good deal of interest recently in our trading relations with the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom has always been a very important market for Canadian raw materials and foodstuffs which Britain requires in great volume. For a wide range of such products Canada is Britain's nearest, and most reliable and cheapest source. As a result, our sales to Britain over the years have normally exceeded her sales to Canada.
In the last three years this excess has been increased because United Kingdom export markets in Canada were adversely affected, first by the devaluation of the Canadian dollar in 1962, and then by the Canadian import surcharges that were in effect for some nine months.
Understandably the British are concerned about the large deficit in their trade with Canada. We can appreciate this because we face the same sort of problem, but in a more exaggerated form, in our current account transactions with the United States. It would
DEBATES	431
The Budget-Mr. Gordon be better in both cases if increased exports enabled these large bilateral deficits to be reduced.
I am glad to note that for a good many products the United Kingdom has now significantly improved its position in this market. For 1964 as a whole its merchandise exports to Canada were $60 million more than in 1963. This improvement is reflected in a variety of British exports to Canada, of which automobiles are one of the most notable examples. Our imports of cars from Britain in 1964 increased by 100 per cent over 1963. Here is a real example of energetic British exporters adapting their products and their dealer and service organizations to meet the needs of Canadian consumers. We expect now to see further substantial improvement in the sale of British products in the Canadian market.
Federal-Provincial Relations
The achievement of Canada's economic goals-of our potential growth-will require the use of the whole range of policies available to us and to provincial governments and local authorities. These include not only general policies, fiscal and monetary, trade and industrial, but also particular policies. These particular policies are reflected in measures relating to the development and use of our natural resources, the education and training of our young people, the planning and proper use of our land, the develpment and the redevelopment of our cities and towns, and the proper planning and building of the roads and other utilities on which both our production and our living are dependent. That is necessary if business, labour, agriculture and other private interests are to play their full part in carrying forward the progress of our economy, and improving our productivity.
All this implies that the federal government must work with the provincial governments and that the latter, in turn, must work not only with us, but with the municipalities. The federal government's responsibility in the field of fiscal policy, monetary policy and trade policy is primary and indisputable. And that is as it should be. To work to best advantage, however, such policies should be co-ordinated with plans and policies in areas which come under provincial jurisdiction.
Moreover, we must recognize that the sum total of the effects of the fiscal policies of the provinces is also of national importance. The provinces and the municipalities
April 26, 1965

The Budget-Mr. Gordon together are now spending more than is the federal government. It follows that changes in provincial revenues and expenditures, and in their budgetary balance, have a major effect upon growth and stability in the Canadian economy. It follows too that the timing of their expenditure measures can be such as to contribute to a steady growth of production and jobs, or the reverse.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
An essential part of the job of good economic management in Canada is to achieve a reasonable harmony in the policies of the different governments. That is why we spend much of our time, both Ministers and officials, in consultation with the provinces. For example, the Provincial Treasurers and Ministers of Finance met with me in what might be called a pre-budget meeting in December, in order that we might jointly review the state of the economy and compare our views as to its prospects.
During the next 18 months, the federal government and the provinces must also review and revise the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements between them in order that we can propose legislation for the five-year period commencing in 1967. It was for that purpose that the federal-provincial conference last year appointed the Tax Structure Committee of Ministers from Ottawa and from the provincial governments. The representatives of the eleven governments will examine the fiscal outlook of federal and provincial governments in an effort to determine the probable requirements of each of them in the six years ahead. We shall endeavour to find a division of the tax fields and a formula for equalizing fiscal capacity which will assure to Parliament and to each provincial legislature effective means of carrying out its own responsibilities under the Constitution.
Royal Commission on Taxation
During the same time that we are discussing and revising our fiscal arrangements with the provinces, we shall be making a thorough review of our own federal tax system-both in its general plan and in detail-with the aid of the report of the Royal Commission on Taxation appointed in September, 1962. Last year I said I expected the report would be published in time to find some reflection in this year's budget. Unfortunately the Commission was not able to conclude its work when it planned to do so, and now I do not expect the report to

be available before fall. Consequently we are having to defer the thorough review of our tax laws until later.
University Finance
This government, as well as its two predecessors, has taken a vital interest in doing what it properly could to help young Canadians to be trained to work effectively in the modern world. Our program of assistance to the provinces for technical and vocational training now involves annual expenditures of over one hundred million dollars. Parliament last year provided for youth allowances to young people of 16 and 17, and also instituted with the co-operation of the provinces a large and already successful program of guaranteed student loans. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been making loans to universities for student residences that are helping to transform the character as well as increase the size of our universities. We are paying unconditional grants equivalent to $2 per capita to the universities in nine provinces and providing the equivalent in Quebec by a tax abatement formula. We are making large grants to universities for scientific research. It is evident, however, that more needs to be done in financing higher education in Canada, though just what should be done and in what way are unresolved questions.
The universities have established their own committee of enquiry into university finance which should be reporting later this year. Its report should be of much help in re-appraising not only what is needed but how it should be supplied. We shall be anxious to discuss the subject of university finance with the provincial governments when there has been an opportunity to study the forthcoming report of Dean Bladen and his colleagues.
Accounts for 1964-65
1 come now to review briefly the outcome of our budgeting for the past year and assess the prospects for the year ahead, before putting the government's proposals before you. The figures are all given in part 2 of the White Paper which I tabled two weeks ago and I will refer only to the highlights. Revenues exceeded all expectations because of the excellent improvement in the economic situation, a greater improvement than I could properly forecast a year ago. At $7,136 million they were $436 million more than the figure in last year's budget. Expenditures are
April 28, 1965	COMMONS
estimated at $7,219 million, $64 million, or less than one per cent, higher than originally forecast. This leaves a budgetary deficit of $83 million, less than one-fifth the amount originally forecast.
Last year, for the first time, I included with the budget a forecast of our revenues and expenditures in terms of the national economic accounts. Part 1 of the White Paper explains the nature of these accounts and gives some of the figures for past years, and for the calendar year 1964. For the past fiscal year our revenues are estimated in these terms at $8,313 million and our expenditures at $7,981 million. This means that in place of the small deficit originally anticipated, in these terms, the national economic accounts reflect a federal government surplus of $332 million.
These results-a deficit of $83 million by our parliamentary public accounts, and a surplus of $332 million by the national economic accounts-are the best in seven years. In practical terms it seems fair to say that after a long period of troublesome deficits the nation's finances are now under firm control.
In this new fiscal year we can anticipate further increases in our revenues based upon the growth to be expected in the economy itself. We can be confident that the recent rates of economic growth will continue well into the summer, although the outlook for the latter part of the year is less certain. We can reasonably forecast an increase of about 7 per cent in the Gross National Product in 1965 compared with 1964, of which increase nearly 5 per cent would be in volume. This will mean that for the first time the Gross National Product of Canada this year will exceed $50 billion.
Outlook for Revenue and Expenditure
Without any changes in our tax laws I would expect our revenues to be about $7,525 million. With the consent of the House I would propose to include a table in Hansard at this point giving the details of this forecast, and comparing them with the estimated figures for last year.
